Metrics alone cannot show which downstream hop caused a slow request. Relevant ideas: trace/span context; W3C headers; sampling; baggage caution; counter/histogram/gauge; labels cardinality. Instrument frameworks, propagate context, export to a backend, and sample appropriately. High sampling costs money; too low misses rare bugs. Tail-based sampling helps.
BE-A-0054.integrationProcedure: 1) Add OTel SDK. 2) Propagate headers. 3) Sample. 4) Link logs via trace_id. 5) Create service maps.
BE-A-0054.example:
// OTel Node auto-instrument Nest/HTTP and export OTLP

http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{path="/orders",status="200"}

BE-A-0071.shortAnswer: Structured logging emits JSON fields (level, msg, requestId, userId) for queryable observability.
BE-A-0071.answer: Answering “A service has p99 latency spikes but low average latency. Explain how you would use traces, metrics, logs, queueing theory, and dependency data to find the cause.?”: Structured logging emits JSON fields (level, msg, requestId, userId) for queryable observability. String-only logs are hard to filter and correlate during incidents. Relevant ideas: JSON logs; levels; PII redaction; correlation ids; generate at edge; propagate headers. Use pino/winston JSON, include requestIds, redact secrets/PII, and ship to a log backend. Debug logs in prod explode cost; sample or raise levels carefully.
BE-A-0071.integrationProcedure: 1) JSON logger. 2) Field standard. 3) Redaction. 4) Ship to stack. 5) Dashboards/alerts.

BE-A-0072.shortAnswer: Multi-tenant SaaS serves many customers with isolation via tenant_id, schemas, or separate databases.
BE-A-0072.answer: Answering “Design a multi-tenant SaaS backend with strong tenant isolation and explain trade-offs between shared schema, separate schemas, and separate databases.?”: Multi-tenant SaaS serves many customers with isolation via tenant_id, schemas, or separate databases. Missing tenant filters leak data across customers—the worst class of bug. Relevant ideas: tenant context; row-level filters; isolation levels; per-tenant limits; principal id; resource tenant/owner. Resolve tenant per request, enforce filters in data layer, test cross-tenant access attempts, and isolate noisy neighbors. Shared DB is cheaper; separate DBs isolate better at higher cost. pen-test with another tenant's IDs; must 404/403.
BE-A-0072.integrationProcedure: 1) Tenant context middleware. 2) Enforce in repo layer. 3) Automated cross-tenant tests. 4) Quotas. 5) Audit logs.
BE-A-0072.example:
WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2

if (order.userId !== user.id) throw new ForbiddenException();

BE-A-0073.shortAnswer: Rate limiting caps request rates per key (IP/user/API key) to protect availability and control abuse.
BE-A-0073.answer: Answering “Design a notification platform that delivers email, SMS, and push notifications with retries, rate limits, deduplication, provider failover, and user preferences.?”: Rate limiting caps request rates per key (IP/user/API key) to protect availability and control abuse. Unauthenticated expensive endpoints get DoSed or scraped. Relevant ideas: token bucket/fixed window; key choice; 429 + Retry-After; distributed stores; closed/open/half-open; error thresholds. Apply limits at edge/API gateway and app, return 429 with headers, and store counters in Redis for multi-node. Strict limits protect systems but can block NAT users sharing IPs—prefer user keys when authenticated. If limit not enforced across nodes, local memory store—move to Redis.
BE-A-0073.integrationProcedure: 1) Identify expensive routes. 2) Redis-backed limits. 3) 429 headers. 4) Tune with product. 5) Monitor.

BE-A-0074.shortAnswer: At-least-once delivery means consumers may see duplicates after retries; handlers must be idempotent.
BE-A-0074.answer: Answering “Design an exactly-once business outcome on top of at-least-once message delivery.?”: At-least-once delivery means consumers may see duplicates after retries; handlers must be idempotent. Assuming exactly-once without a dedupe store double-charges or double-emails. Relevant ideas: acks/retries; idempotency keys; dedupe stores; poison messages; Idempotency-Key; dedupe store. Acknowledge only after durable side effects, store processed keys, and send poison messages to DLQ. Exactly-once is rare/expensive; usually at-least-once + idempotency is the practical design. If duplicates appear, add idempotency table unique constraints.
BE-A-0074.integrationProcedure: 1) Make handlers idempotent. 2) Persist dedupe keys. 3) DLQ. 4) Metric retries/dupes.
BE-A-0074.example:
INSERT INTO processed_events(id) VALUES($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; -- skip if not inserted

UNIQUE(user_id, idempotency_key)
-- return stored response when key exists

BE-A-0075.shortAnswer: A modular monolith is a single deployable with strong internal module boundaries—often the best step before microservices.
BE-A-0075.answer: Answering “Explain how you would split a modular monolith into services only when organizational and runtime boundaries justify it.?”: A modular monolith is a single deployable with strong internal module boundaries—often the best step before microservices. Microservices too early multiply ops cost without real team/scale need. Relevant ideas: module boundaries; no cross-DB joins secretly; clear APIs; extract later; data ownership; API contracts. Enforce module public APIs, separate schemas if needed, and forbid deep imports via lint. One deploy is simple; still requires discipline or it becomes a monolith ball of mud. If modules circularly import, boundaries are wrong—revisit context map.
BE-A-0075.integrationProcedure: 1) Define modules. 2) Lint boundaries. 3) Separate tables ownership. 4) Extract service only with evidence.
BE-A-0075.example:
orders/ public API only; inventory/ cannot import orders/internal/*

// orders service owns orders tables; inventory exposes ReserveStock API/events
